newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian local elections yield mixed results.
newsitem.headline: Italian local elections yield mixed results.

text.p: Italy's governing centre-left coalition suffered a setback as results showed opposition candidates leading the first round of mayoral elections in two big northern cities, but made stronger showings in other areas.

Most of the elections in more than 100 cities and towns with a population of more than 15,000 will have to go to a run-off on May 11. Run-offs will not be held in some 1,000 smaller towns and villages.
The Sunday polls strengthened the hand of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, on which Prodi's leftist government relies to survive.
The vote saw a major drubbing of the separatist Northern League, whose incumbent mayor Marco Formentini did not make the run-off in Milan, the country's northern financial capital.
The League also also suffered setbacks in elections for six provincial council presidencies, losing control of three.
Both the centre left and centre right claimed victory.
"It's difficult to say who has won and who has lost," said a commentator on state television RAI.
"The results have to be studied without warfare," said Massimo D'Alema, head of the Democratic Party of the Left, the largest party in Prodi's coalition.
He said the centre left had gained overall if results were compared with those of the 1996 general elections, which it won.

The centre left suffered big setbacks in the prize northern cities of Milan and Turin, where mayoral candidates backed by former Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi's opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance took the first round lead.
"We will go on to the run-off elections and see to it that the red power doesn't continue to run the cities," he said.

The centre left led in Ancona and Trieste and its candidates won on the first round in Belluno, Siena and southern Reggio Calabria. With most results in, D'Alema's PDS had the largest share of the vote, with about 17 percent.
The largest winners in Berlusconi's opposition were the right-wing National Alliance with some 12 percent and Berlusconi's own Forza Italia party, with about 10 percent.

The centre right's good showing in Milan and Turin galvanised Berlusconi to declare war on the government, indicating that his alliance would not make any deals to help Prodi enact vital structural measures to cut spending.

"I say it as leader of the Alliance and leader of the Forza Italia party (that) we won't give one vote to help this government. For the good of the country, this government has to go," he told reporters.

He was apparently responding to comments in Washington by Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini that cuts in social spending, including on pensions, had to be made even if that meant breaking Prodi's parliamentary majority.
Prodi's centre-left government relies on the hard-left Communist Refoundation party for its majority in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house).
But Refoundation is opposed to social spending cuts that the coalition says are necessary to haul the country into the founding group for Europe's planned single currency.
Berlusconi, who was prime minister in 1994, had said previously he would be willing to back Prodi on economic policy if the government ditched Refoundation as an ally.
But he appeared to rule out future deals after the weekend vote. "They have slammed the door in our face every time we have shown willingness to reason together," Berlusconi said.
Commentators said Communist Refoundation's own good showing, with about 8.2 percent in the mayoral races, complicated matters for Prodi.
The party indicated that it could seek a high price for backing centre-left candidates in second round voting in cities where the centre right was leading after the first round.
"Given that we got so many votes, this will give more importance to both our social spending and structural reform position," party leader Fausto Bertinotti told Reuters.
